titleStmt.title: The emotional valence and features of subliminal priming images impact conscious perception of face expressions
titleStmt.author: Huang
Rana
Vaina

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: The emotional valence and features of subliminal priming images impact conscious perception of face expressions

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Priming images containing a face compared to those not containing a face significantly impaired performance on neutral or angry targetface evaluation.

span.label: subliminal affective priming of facial expression perception
span.quote: The SAFFIMAP test assesses the effect of subliminally-presented affective priming images on the perception of a target-face expression (neutral or angry).

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: Subjects responded to the emotion portrayed in a pixelated target-face by indicating via key-press if the expression was angry or neutral.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: faces in the prime are processed preferentially, and the perceived prime face then competes with and interferes with perception of the target face
span.quote: This suggest that processing of faces occurs preferentially to the processing of non-face containing images, and that the face perceived in the priming image interferes with the ability to perceive the target-face expression.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: a face in the prime sets up an expectation of an emotionally charged target, which speeds and biases the response toward 'angry'
span.quote: Taken together these results suggest that the face in the prime image prompts the viewer to expect an emotionally charged target-face, which quickens (see Supplement D) and biases the response towards the angry rather than neutral-target face.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: an egocentric vantage-point recruits action-preparation processes, which lower the priority given to affect processing and so degrade angry-face recognition
span.note: status: the paper's own words: we suggest that
span.quote: From this result, we suggest that, because of the direct relevance of the egocentric vantage-point to the viewer, the egocentric prime image may engage a series of processes relevant to potential action preparation, which could weaken the priority of affective processing, and thus interfere with the ability to recognize the angry target-face expression.

span.label: The design cannot separate the emotion of the depicted scene from the emotion of the facial expression within the prime; the authors state they will add further prime dimensions to do so.
span.quote: We will extend this study by adding additional dimensions to the priming stimuli, to dissociate between the emotion of the scene and that of the facial expressions.

span.label: prime and mask both subtending 12.5 by 12.5 degrees and presented at the same central location
span.note: eliminates: a size or position difference between prime and mask, which would make the masking incomplete in a way that varies with the stimulus
span.quote: Both the prime and the mask subtended 12.5x12.5 degrees, and were presented in the same spatial location at the center of the computer screen.

span.label: subliminal priming
span.quote: Our results suggest that the content of the priming image (presence of a face) and its vantage-point (egocentric or allocentric) impacts the effect of affective subliminal priming on the evaluation of facial expressions

span.label: affective primacy
span.quote: the affective primacy hypothesis which predicts that affective information can be accessed automatically, preceding conscious cognition, holds true in subliminal priming only when the priming image contains a face

span.label: centricity
span.quote: Regardless of whether the prime image contained a face, there was a significant effect of the centricity of the image on the evaluation of the target-face expression

span.label: egocentric
span.quote: For egocentric primes, recognition of neutral target-face expressions was significantly better than of angry expressions

span.label: A NAMED HYPOTHESIS GIVEN A BOUNDARY CONDITION RATHER THAN A VERDICT: `the AFFECTIVE PRIMACY HYPOTHESIS which predicts that affective information can be accessed automatically, preceding conscious cognition, HOLDS TRUE IN SUBLIMINAL PRIMING ONLY WHEN THE PRIMING IMAGE CONTAINS A FACE.` Not confirmed, not refuted - restricted. **And the condition is a property of the STIMULUS**, where Q-787's ambiguity condition is a property of the outcome situation and Holcomb2005's is a property of the observer. Three different places a priming effect can be conditional, and a corpus that records only `X primes Y` loses all three
span.quote: the affective primacy hypothesis which predicts that affective information can be accessed automatically, preceding conscious cognition, holds true in subliminal priming only when the priming image contains a face

span.label: THE PRIME MAKES THE TASK HARDER, WHICH IS THE CASE THE STANDARD DEFINITION EXCLUDES. `Subliminally priming with a face-containing image SIGNIFICANTLY IMPAIRS the subjects' ability to perceive the emotional expression of the target-face.` Minton2017 (Q-780) quotes McNamara defining priming as `an IMPROVEMENT in performance` and then strikes the word out, because `priming can also involve a change in performance that is neutral or results in POORER performance`. **This record is the counterexample that correction needed** - a real interference effect, in a different literature, from a paper that never mentions the definitional dispute
span.quote: Our first notable finding is that subliminally priming with a face-containing image significantly impairs the subjects’ ability to perceive the emotional expression of the target-face

span.label: IT CONTRADICTS A NAMED STUDY AND SAYS SO PLAINLY: `This result is AT ODDS WITH the findings of Andrews et al. (2011), who reported that there was NO subliminal affective priming effect when priming with emotional facial expressions.` And it offers the reconciling detail rather than leaving the disagreement bare - `the emotional expression of a face in a prime can be processed, AT LEAST PARTIALLY, during a 16 ms exposure`. A null and a positive on the same manipulation, with an exposure duration between them
span.quote: This result is at odds with the findings of Andrews et al. (2011), who reported that there was no subliminal affective priming effect when priming with emotional facial expressions

span.label: AND THE CONGRUENCY EFFECT IS ITSELF CONDITIONAL, WHICH IS THE SECOND `ONLY WHEN` IN ONE PAPER: `we found that specifically the INCONGRUENCY of the pleasant prime and the angry expression of the target-face lead to worse performance ... DIFFERING FROM THESE STUDIES, we found that this effect occurred ONLY WHEN THE PRIME IMAGE CONTAINED A FACE.` So the paper reports an affective congruency effect, agrees it is the known one, and then restricts it - twice qualifying a borrowed finding rather than claiming a new one
span.quote: Differing from these studies, we found that this effect occurred only when the prime image contained a face

span.label: extends → Vaina, Rana, Cotos Cheng, Huang, & Podea (2014) preliminary study of affective subliminal priming in schizophrenic subjects
span.quote: Using the same experimental protocol as in our previous study (Vaina et al., 2014), here we investigate in young healthy subjects how the affective content of the priming image, the presence of a face or the vantage-point of the prime content (image centricity) impact the effect of affective subliminal priming on the identification of target-face expressions.

span.label: contradicts → Andrews, Lipp, Malan, & Könjg (2011)
span.quote: This result is at odds with the findings of Andrews et al. (2011), who reported that there was no subliminal affective priming effect when priming with emotional facial expressions (Andrews, Lipp, Malan, & Könjg, 2011).

span.label: builds-on → Kemps, Erauw, and Vandierendock (1996)
span.quote: This result is in agreement with Kemps, Erauw, and Vandierendock (1996) finding that facial expressions influenced the liking rating of Korean ideographs at exposure duration of 30 ms and longer, while pictures without faces did not elicit an affective reaction until they were presented for at least 100 ms.

span.label: subliminal priming —operationalised-as→ affective primacy
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — THE HYPOTHESIS IS TESTED THROUGH THE PARADIGM, and the `ONLY WHEN` is inside the quote - an edge reading `subliminal priming operationalises affective primacy` without it would state the general claim the paper spent four studies restricting. Weight 0.85: the restriction is this paper's contribution, so the unqualified relation is precisely what it does not support.
span.quote: the affective primacy hypothesis which predicts that affective information can be accessed automatically, preceding conscious cognition, holds true in subliminal priming only when the priming image contains a face

span.label: egocentric —causes→ subliminal priming
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — NO `effect_direction`. Vantage-point is a two-level CATEGORY (egocentric or allocentric), not a quantity, so `increases` and `reduces` are both meaningless - what the paper reports is that the two levels DIFFER, and in which direction for which target. And what this edge cannot carry is the sharpest part: the centricity effect holds `REGARDLESS of whether the prime image contained a face`, which makes it the one route here that does NOT need the affective content. That sentence never says `subliminal priming`, so it is on the `centricity` concept row instead.
span.quote: Our results suggest that the content of the priming image (presence of a face) and its vantage-point (egocentric or allocentric) impacts the effect of affective subliminal priming on the evaluation of facial expressions

span.label: generalized linear mixed model
span.quote: We applied a General Linear Mixture Model (GLMM) to model the effect of the priming categories (affective category, face content (face present vs. face absent), and centricity) and the target-face (angry vs. neutral) on the evaluation of the target-face expression via a probit-link function, due to the binary response variable (correct vs. incorrect).

span.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
span.quote: Post hoc tests were conducted through the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank (WSR) Test, where pair-wise comparisons were conducted among average performance within categories between each subject.

span.label: false discovery rate correction
span.quote: Significance scores from WSR were FDR-corrected at a false discovery rate of 0.05.

span.label: power analysis
span.quote: We determined that a sample size of at least 28 subjects would be sufficient to reach a power of 0.80, from an a priori power analysis using G*Power.

span.label: F-test
span.note: about this quote: QUOTE RECOVERED FROM THE PAPER'S OWN CHARACTERS (Q-701). The recorded quote was LETTERS-ONLY IDENTICAL to this stretch of the staged text but not an exact substring of it - spaces, hyphens, ligature glyphs or mathematical operators differed, so it could never anchor. This is the file's own text between the same two letters: not produced by a rule about the damage, copied out of the file. Round-trip checked (the recovered span is letters-only equal to the original) and length-checked. The text as originally recorded is kept in `evidence_as_extracted`.
span.quote: The presence or absence of a face in the priming images significantly affected subjects’ evaluation of the target-face (GLMM, F(1,2976) = 6.186, p = 0.013

span.label: standard error
span.quote: In trials where primes contained a face, subjects were poorer at correctly identifying the emotion expressed in the target face, compared to when the prime image did not contain a face. (face: μ = 74.20%, se = 1.79%; non-face: μ = 78.00%, se = 1.49%) (WRS, z=-2.266, p = 0.023)

span.label: Priming images that contained a face impaired subsequent identification of the target face's expression relative to primes without a face.
span.quote: Priming images containing a face compared to those not containing a face significantly impaired performance on neutral or angry targetface evaluation.

span.label: Pleasant primes containing a face selectively damaged recognition of angry target-face expressions.
span.quote: Recognition of angry target-face expressions was selectively impaired by pleasant prime images which contained a face.

span.label: After an egocentric prime, neutral target expressions were recognised significantly better than angry ones.
span.quote: For egocentric primes, recognition of neutral target-face expressions was significantly better than of angry expressions.

span.label: Among face-containing primes, neutral ones produced better target-face performance than either aggressive or pleasant ones.
span.quote: Subjects performed better on perceiving target-face expressions when the affective value of the face-containing prime image was neutral compared to aggressive or pleasant (neutral vs. aggressive: WRS, z = 2.060, p = 0.039) (neutral vs. pleasant: WRS, z = 1.966, p = 0.049).

span.label: The authors conclude that the affective primacy hypothesis survives in subliminal priming only in the special case where the prime image contains a face.
span.quote: Our results suggest that, first, the affective primacy hypothesis which predicts that affective information can be accessed automatically, preceding conscious cognition, holds true in subliminal priming only when the priming image contains a face.

span.label: The face-versus-non-face prime difference reached significance only for aggressive prime content.
span.quote: was significant only when the affective content of the prime image was aggressive (aggressive, face: μ = 73.4%, se = 1.99%; aggressive, non-face: μ = 81.0%, se = 1.85%) (WRS, z = -3.835, p = 0.001).

span.label: congruency effect
span.quote: Numerous subliminal priming experiments (Klinger, Burton, & Pitts, 2000; Neumann & Lozo, 2012; Otten & Wentura, 1999), showed that affectively congruent prime-target pairs facilitate either response time or evaluation of the target stimulus. This is referred to as the congruency effect.

span.label: affective primacy hypothesis
span.quote: The affective primacy hypothesis (Zajonc, 1980) proposes that affective information can be accessed automatically, and precedes conscious cognition.

span.label: SAFFIMAP (Subliminal Affective Image Priming) test
span.quote: The SAFFIMAP test assesses the effect of subliminally-presented affective priming images on the perception of a target-face expression (neutral or angry).

span.label: centricity of an image (egocentric vs. allocentric vantage-point)
span.term: centricity of an image (egocentric vs. allocentric vantage-point)
span.quote: The priming images were broadly categorised as aggressive, pleasant, or neutral and further subcategorised by the presence of a face and by the centricity (egocentric or allocentric vantage-point) of the image content.

span.label: affective category of the priming image (aggressive, pleasant, neutral)
span.term: affective category of the priming image (aggressive, pleasant, neutral)
span.quote: The priming images used in this experiment were categorised by their affect (aggressive, pleasant, or neutral), and further sub-categorised by the vantage-point of the image content (egocentric or allocentric) and the presence or absence of a face.

span.label: presence or absence of a face in the priming image
span.term: presence or absence of a face in the priming image
span.quote: We applied a General Linear Mixture Model (GLMM) to model the effect of the priming categories (affective category, face content (face present vs. face absent), and centricity) and the target-face (angry vs. neutral) on the evaluation of the target-face expression via a probit-link function, due to the binary response variable (correct vs. incorrect).

span.label: centricity (vantage-point) of the priming image
span.quote: The priming images were broadly categorised as aggressive, pleasant, or neutral and further subcategorised by the presence of a face and by the centricity (egocentric or allocentric vantage-point) of the image content.

span.label: accuracy of target-face expression identification (percent correct)
span.term: accuracy of target-face expression identification (percent correct)
span.quote: For the SAFFIMAP test, both percent correct (described below) and reaction time (shown in Supplement D) were acquired.

span.label: between-subject variability
span.quote: Subject variability was treated as a random effect in the GLMM.

span.label: 16 ms — exposure duration of the subliminal prime image, followed by a 100 ms mask
span.quote: Next, a priming image, randomly selected from the experimental database, was shown for 16 ms and immediately followed by a mask displayed for 100 ms.

span.label: Thirty-three subjects — number of participants, with their sex split and mean age
span.quote: Thirty-three subjects (17 females, mean age = 18.17 years, SD ± 1.49) participated in the study.

span.label: 120 trials — total number of trials in the SAFFIMAP test
span.note: about this quote: QUOTE RECOVERED FROM THE PAPER'S OWN CHARACTERS (Q-701). The recorded quote was LETTERS-ONLY IDENTICAL to this stretch of the staged text but not an exact substring of it - spaces, hyphens, ligature glyphs or mathematical operators differed, so it could never anchor. This is the file's own text between the same two letters: not produced by a rule about the damage, copied out of the file. Round-trip checked (the recovered span is letters-only equal to the original) and length-checked. The text as originally recorded is kept in `evidence_as_extracted`.
span.quote: The next trial began immediately after the subject’s response, or after 4000 ms, if no response was entered. There were in total 120 trials

span.label: 74.20% vs 78.00% — mean accuracy on target-face evaluation after face primes versus non-face primes
span.quote: In trials where primes contained a face, subjects were poorer at correctly identifying the emotion expressed in the target face, compared to when the prime image did not contain a face. (face: μ = 74.20%, se = 1.79%; non-face: μ = 78.00%, se = 1.49%) (WRS, z=-2.266, p = 0.023)

span.label: 73.4% vs 81.0% — mean accuracy after aggressive primes with a face versus aggressive primes without a face
span.quote: was significant only when the affective content of the prime image was aggressive (aggressive, face: μ = 73.4%, se = 1.99%; aggressive, non-face: μ = 81.0%, se = 1.85%) (WRS, z = -3.835, p = 0.001).

span.label: 81.64% vs 77.31% — mean accuracy on neutral target faces after egocentric versus allocentric primes
span.quote: egocentric compared to when it was allocentric (egocentric: μ = 81.64%, se = 2.03%; allocentric: μ = 77.31%, se = 2.05%) (WRS, z = -2.215, p = 0.017).
